vipra
(‘one in whom [the seed of धर्म] has sprouted’)
------------------------------------------
A ब्राह्मण is known by several names, one of which is the word विप्र. The Ṛgveda (10.112.9) uses this word as applied to the deity गणपति.
Etymologically, it means one in whom the seed of धर्म has already sprouted.
In a more technical sense, he is a ब्राह्मण who has undergone the necessary sacraments and is also endowed with the विद्या or knowledge of the scriptures. He is expected to discharge six duties: yajana (performing a sacrifice); yājana (conducting a sacrifice for others); adhya-yana (studying the scriptures); adhyāpana (teaching the scriptures to others); दान (giving gifts to others); and, pratigraha (accepting gifts in accordance with धर्म).
These six are called the षट्कर्मस् for a ब्राह्मण.
The tree अश्वत्थ (Ficus religiosa) is also known by this name and considered worthy of worship like a ब्राह्मण.

viparyaya
(‘contrariety’)
------------------------------------------
This is a technical term used in the Yogasūtras (1.6, 8).
The cittavṛttis or the modifications of the मिन्द्, though they appear to be infinite, can be classified into five groups: pramāṇa (means of valid knowledge), विपर्यय (contrariety), विकल्प (mere concept), निद्रा (sleep) and स्मृति (memory).
Viparyaya, the second, is defined as mithyājñāna—false knowledge—not based on reality. When, in twilight, we see a snake in a rope lying on the ground, it is विपर्यय, seeing one thing for another.
Avidyā is another name for it.

Vipāśā
(‘without bonds’)
------------------------------------------
The Ṛgveda (3.33.1 and 3; 4.30.11) mentions the river Vipāṭ or Vipāś. It has been identified with the modern Beas river in the Punjab.
According to the Mahābhārata, when the demon कल्माषपाद devoured वसिष्ठ’s son शक्ति, वसिष्ठ tried to commit सुइचिदे (due to intense sorrow) by tying himself with ropes and falling into this river, then known as Uruñjirā. Being afraid of incurring the sin of killing a ब्राह्मण sage, the river (or the presiding goddess of the river) unbounded him and carried him to the bank. Hence वसिष्ठ gave it the name विपाशा (that which freed him from the bonds; पाश = bond) (Mahābhārata, Ādiparva 177.6).

vipāka
(‘ripening’)
------------------------------------------
In general, this word means the ripening state. However, it is used more in a technical sense as कर्मविपाक or the ripening of कर्म (actions about to give their results).
According to the Yogasūtras (2.13) of पतञ्जलि (200 B. C.) विपाक of a कर्म results in three things: जाति (birth in a particular species of living beings); āyus (duration of life); भोग (experience of good and bad results).
See also KARMAVIPĀKA.
In the ancient medical sciences, the word was used to indicate the state of digestion of ड़ोओद्.
